item.title: A DevOps engineer and an AI dive headfirst into business tasks.
item.description:
Here is the English translation of the provided Russian text, keeping technical terms as requested:

209 thousand product items across 150 branches are recorded differently, and a regular join matches at most 1% of them. Data engineer Dmitry Dunaev at the Slerm Evening School showed how this mess was cleaned up using LLMs, embeddings, and fuzzy search, while also freeing managers from making 5-minute calls from an endless call list.

Of the 15 models tested, only one showed the necessary balance of criteria. Which one and why, we analyze in the conference summary along with a checklist on when it's worth building an agent and when it's better to save the money.

item.title: Local LLM migration Vertica2Trino. How to get it to a working state if the model can't handle it?
item.description:
Hi, this is the BI development team from the commercial department: Alexey Dubinets and Pavel Bespalov. 

In this article, we'll tell you how we built a migration pipeline for our data marts using a local LLM. 

Let me clarify right away: this is not a story about how we used Codex or Claude Code, wrote a skill, and got a magical result. We'll show the engineering side of the task: where the local model fails, which naive solutions don't work, and what we had to build around it to make the translation reproducible.

item.title: AI was used to verify the most complex mathematical proof to date.
item.description:
An important milestone in mathematical research using AI was the example of the team from Axiom Math, which for the first time automatically verified the proof of a theorem concerning prime numbers — colloquially known as "Theorem 246" — using its own artificial intelligence system, AxiomProver.

During formal verification, mathematicians task a computer with checking a machine-readable version of the proof. This process does not provide a 100% guarantee of the proof's correctness, as shown by a recent demonstration in which it was revealed that an error in the method could lead to false confirmation of an AI-generated proof. Nevertheless, this computational method brings the approval of a proof using AI as close to reality as possible.

This confirmation formalizes an important breakthrough in number theory. Beyond this specific proof, it demonstrates how automated AI-assisted verification could be used in the future to ensure the correctness of AI-generated computer code, which will soon become the foundation of software worldwide.

Read more

item.title: Modders hacked DLSS 5 and stuffed it into everything — from Skyrim to GTA San Andreas.
item.description:
Sometimes something super-mega-secret leaks out not through a leak, but simply because someone forgot to remove one file from the build. Well, they forgot, it happens to everyone.

That's exactly what happened last week with DLSS 5 – the controversial thing from Nvidia. There was no official announcement, but there was an early version of the game NBA 2K27, which contained an inconspicuous DLL file nvngx_dlssnr.dll weighing 158 megabytes... and off it went.

Within days, modders had applied neural network rendering to a good three dozen games, from Cyberpunk 2077 to GTA San Andreas, which is already twenty years old (though the remaster is a bit younger).

If you've been following DLSS 5 since March, you remember all those memes and hate. Let's try to figure out what happened, how it works technically, what the tests show, and why people are still arguing about the fate of the gaming industry. I'll also throw in some pictures and videos, because this is one of those cases where seeing once is better than reading a hundred times.

Read more

item.title: The agents completed the task. Why is the test still failed?
item.description:
Suppose you have several AI agents. One handles a ticket, another modifies code, a third runs tests, and a fourth prepares a release.

The task is closed, tests are green, the artifact is built. The success_rate metric shows success.

Can we celebrate?

Not necessarily. The agents might have performed the same work multiple times, violated the order of operations, simultaneously grabbed a shared resource, or accidentally achieved the correct result through an invalid sequence of actions.

The final state is correct. The process is not.

This is exactly the problem that CoCoBench — a new benchmark for evaluating the coordination of multiple AI agents — aims to measure. It was developed by researchers from Nanjing University, Tsinghua, and AgiBot.

The main idea of the research is useful far beyond robotics:

item.title: Mobile audio guide or how I made an app for self-guided city walks
item.description:
I continue to talk about the results of my Means of Small Automation, or about the fact that today almost anyone can personally create the application they need for themselves.

One day I was walking through the city’s backstreets. Old buildings full of history. And I absolutely love history. Whose house it is, when it was built, who lived there, and what else is interesting. There’s no plaque on the facade, no tour guide materializes next to me. Constantly pulling out my phone, searching online, opening several websites—that’s quite a chore. You could take a photo of the building and figure it out later. But “later” almost never comes.

That’s how the idea for Yerick City Explorer was born—an Android app for independent city walks.

item.title: AI detectors. Are we on the path to a world of dystopias?
item.description:
```html

Introduction. No neural networks were used in writing this opus.

Setup. I sometimes share my expert observations on a topic I’ve been working on for over 10 years. Among other things, I occasionally use neural networks for two tasks: searching for new information that might have slipped past me, and final text polishing before publication to make complex text more reader-friendly.

The other day, on one platform, moderators removed an article with the note “Generated text.” And when I sent a request to technical support, three other publications that had garnered over 50,000 views were also banned.

Journalists, representatives of research institutes, and government agencies had reached out to me for permission to use these materials. In other words, there seems to be no question about the level of expertise, but the AI detector somehow fell short... And I became curious to take a more professional look at this beast.

From a standpoint of reasonable logic, it’s important to first agree on what we aim to achieve through the total use of AI detectors. Options: 1. That authors write themselves. Period! 2. That we don’t spawn a billion units of content! 3. That...?

And here I ask myself: what is it that I personally want to get from an article/book/essay? And I answer myself: the pleasure of reading / new important information / a new interesting author or expert to look into. Whether neural networks were used or not is completely irrelevant. “Liked it / didn’t like it — that’s the main criterion!”

item.title: 1C Without Routine: Neural Networks, MCP, Automation, and a Little Solitaire
item.description:
What's happening in the world of 1C? The neural network confidently writes bubble sort, but on a real 1C project it suddenly starts inventing non-existent procedures. An AI agent edits the configuration directly via MCP. Administrators learn to automatically find and restart "stuck processes." And in between all this, you can… play Solitaire right inside 1C.

In the new Knowledge Base digest, we've collected materials that clearly show just how diverse the tasks around 1C can be — from experiments with AI and development automation to quite practical tools for administrators and users.

item.title: Where VLM didn't read old newspapers: breaking down PereStruct, an open dataset and a modular parser
item.description:
Try opening a scan of a Soviet newspaper and reading one article from beginning to end. A person quickly notices the large headline, the continuation in the adjacent column, and the caption under the photo. For an algorithm, what lies before it is a faded page with dozens of tightly packed rectangles, non-standard fonts, and an ambiguous reading order.

Even if OCR correctly recognizes almost all words, the output is still not a document. You need to understand which fragments belong to one article, where its beginning is, in what order to connect the blocks, and what should not be included in the main text.

We developed PereStruct — a modular pipeline for parsing historical newspapers. It combines a layout detector based on YOLO, Yandex Vision OCR, error correction using Yandex AI Studio models, and a separate model for semantic article assembly. Along with the code, we are publishing a labeled dataset and a benchmark so that other teams can study the approach and run experiments on historical documents.

Read more

item.title: From a closed .NET gateway to Java/Kubernetes in 11 hours: a production case study of agentic development.
item.description:
Estimates like "AI speeds up developers by 20-30%" poorly describe what happened to me in one working day. In 11 hours from idea to production cutover: decompilation of a closed-source .NET component, reverse engineering of an undocumented binary protocol from two implementations, a compatible Java implementation, a regression test suite from real traffic, a container, Kubernetes, an independent review, and production cutover. I explain how the work was structured — a virtual engineering team of specialized sub-agents, three independent sources of truth, and an in-house vendor client acting as an external oracle. And why the main accelerator turned out not to be code generation speed.

Read more

item.title: What the free Devin is capable of: a test on a real project
item.description:
Hello, Habr! My name is Zavur, I'm a frontend developer at Selectel. Every day I work in the familiar development environment VS Code. However, in personal projects that I create to explore new tools and methods of writing code, I often use Cursor.

It greatly speeds up development, but I've long wanted to check: is artificial intelligence capable of independently turning a raw idea into a full-fledged working application? Sometimes you want to quickly see a prototype in action to decide whether to develop the project further. That's why I couldn't ignore the promising service Devin.

Let's see what implementing an idea with Devin looks like in practice, and try to figure out whether we are truly looking at a potential competitor to Cursor.
